Mississippi Property Tax Guide: Appeals, Exemptions and Selling With Tax Due

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Property Tax Guide sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Disagreement with a property valuation: request a hearing with the county Board of Supervisors (contact the county Chancery Clerk). (Property Tax FAQ - I disagree with the assessment; source)
  • Assessment ratios are set by the Mississippi Constitution; tax = true value x assessment ratio x millage rate. (Property Tax FAQ - assessment ratio; source)
  • Property taxes are due by February 1 following assessment; if unpaid, penalties and interest accrue. (Local Property Appraisal - Paying Property Taxes; source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How is property tax calculated in Mississippi?

A Mississippi tax bill is the true value of the property times an assessment ratio times the millage rate. The Department of Revenue FAQ gives the formula as true value x assessment ratio x millage rate, and the ratios are set by the Mississippi Constitution.

Property is split into five classes, and the class decides the ratio:

ClassPropertyAssessment ratio
ISingle-family, owner-occupied residential real property10%
IIAll other real property (except Class I or IV)15%
IIIPersonal property (except vehicles and Class IV)15%
IVPublic utility property30%
VMotor vehicles30%

The state's own example uses a $100,000 true value, a 10% ratio and 125 mills, which gives $10,000 of assessed value and $1,250 in tax. One mill is one thousandth of a dollar. A house you live in is Class I. Class I is limited to owner-occupied single-family residences, so property outside that definition, such as land or a rental, is Class II at the higher 15% ratio. Heirs who stop living in a parent's home should ask the Tax Assessor how the house will be classed. See the Department of Revenue appraisal page for the full explanation.

Who sets, bills and collects the tax?

Several locally elected officials share the job, and the state mostly oversees. According to the Department of Revenue, the county Tax Assessor determines value, the Tax Collector collects, the Chancery Clerk keeps land records and runs the tax sale, and the Board of Supervisors hears objections and adopts the tax rolls.

  • Taxing authorities are county boards of supervisors, municipal boards and certain school boards. They set the millage rates.
  • Every property carries a county rate and a school district rate. A property inside city limits or a special levee district pays that jurisdiction's rate too.
  • Each county has five supervisors, one elected from each of five districts.
  • The Department of Revenue audits county appraisal work, and the State Auditor oversees collection.

Tax revenue supports county and city governments and local school districts, and the department says a significant portion of county revenue comes from it. That is why two houses of equal value can have different bills if one is inside a city and the other is not.

When are Mississippi property taxes assessed and due?

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1, bills go out in November or December, and the tax is due by February 1 of the following year. If February 1 lands on a weekend or legal holiday, payment the next Monday carries no penalty or interest.

StepTiming
Assessment date, owner of recordJanuary 1
Homestead exemption filing windowJanuary 1 to April 1
Ownership instrument filed with Chancery Clerk (for exemption)Before January 7
Assessment appeal to Board of SupervisorsNormally by the first Monday in August
Bills issuedNovember to December
Taxes dueFebruary 1 of the next year
County tax saleFirst Monday in April or last Monday in August, depending on county

Assessors must revalue real property at least once every four years, and taxable personal property every year. Interior inspections of residences are not required, but the assessor can physically inspect the property and all structures on it count, including an old barn.

How does the homestead exemption work, and what changes when you sell?

Homestead exemption cuts the tax on a primary residence, and the owner has to apply for it. The Department of Revenue homestead page says applications go to the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and that the exemption renews each year without refiling unless something changes.

  • Tier 1 is a tax credit of up to $300 for applicants under 65 who do not qualify for the disability tier.
  • Tier 2 covers owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, by January 1. They are exempt from tax on the first $7,500 of assessed value, and the state FAQ describes the exemption as covering the first $75,000 of true value.
  • Tier 3 is a total exemption for service-connected totally disabled veterans, honorably discharged veterans at least 90 years old, and certain unremarried surviving spouses of service members who died on active duty.

Applicants must own and occupy the home on January 1, and ownership must exist before then. Changes in ownership, use or occupancy, including deed changes, divorce or death, can require a new application. Failing to keep up with income tax filing or vehicle registration rules can lead to disallowance, and the department warns that a disallowed owner may have to repay the exemption received in error.

For sellers, the timing point is January 1. If a house closes after that date and before the bill is paid, the tax was assessed to the earlier owner of record, so the closing statement should deal with it.

How do you appeal an assessment in Mississippi?

You request a hearing with the county Board of Supervisors, and the Chancery Clerk can tell you how the county handles it. The state FAQ says the appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due.

The Board of Supervisors reviews values set by the Tax Assessor, hears taxpayer objections and adopts the tax rolls. A few practical points follow from the state's materials:

  • The hearing is about the valuation of your property. Millage rates are set separately by the county, city and school district.
  • A wrong square footage can sometimes support a refund for prior years. Ask the Chancery Clerk.
  • A rise in your bill comes from a change in value, a change in the rate, or both.

If you are selling soon, ask the Chancery Clerk and the Tax Collector how a pending appeal is treated, and have the title company confirm the amount owed.

What happens if Mississippi property tax goes unpaid?

Penalties and interest accrue, and a property that stays delinquent is sold at the county tax auction. The Department of Revenue says some counties hold the auction on the first Monday in April and others on the last Monday in August.

The Chancery Clerk administers the annual sale and keeps the records. Properties sold for taxes can be redeemed for a period after the sale, and the clerk can tell you the amount needed. If a property is not purchased at the sale, it goes to the State of Mississippi and is managed by the Secretary of State, whose office can be reached at 1-866-835-2637.

The tax collector is the contact for tax sale questions in the county where the property sits. A seller with delinquent taxes should ask for the delinquent amount and any redemption figure early, so there are no surprises at closing.

What does a Mississippi house seller usually face with property tax?

The recurring issues are an unpaid prior-year bill, a homestead exemption that was lost or never filed, and a possible class change on a house nobody lives in. An heir who inherits a house that is no longer owner-occupied should ask the Tax Assessor whether the class, and so the ratio, changes from 10% to 15% of true value.

  • Pull the tax bill and the legal description from the Tax Collector and Chancery Clerk.
  • Ask whether homestead exemption was claimed and whether any disallowance is pending.
  • Ask the title company to confirm the status of the current year bill and any tax sale history.
  • If the estate is in probate, see our Mississippi probate guide for who can sign.

We buy Mississippi houses as-is, including houses with tax due or deferred repairs, and we reply with a written offer. We make no promise on price in this guide.

More questions about Mississippi Property Tax Guide

What is the Mississippi property tax rate?

There is no single statewide rate. Each property pays a county millage and a school district millage, plus a city or special district rate where one applies. The tax equals true value times the assessment ratio times the millage total, and Class I residences are assessed at 10% of true value.

When are Mississippi property taxes due?

Taxes are due on or before February 1 for property assessed the previous year. If February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the following Monday is the last day without penalty or interest.

Can I appeal my Mississippi property assessment?

Yes. Request a hearing with the county Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk. The appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the due date of the taxes.

When must I apply for homestead exemption in Mississippi?

Applications are taken by the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1. Filing after April 1 does not qualify for that assessment year.

Can I sell a house in Mississippi with property tax due?

Yes. A cash buyer can take the house as-is, and the tax owed is something the title company confirms before closing. If taxes stay delinquent, the property can be sold at the county tax auction, so check the amount and any redemption figure first.

Mississippi Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Mississippi Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Tier 1 regular exemption (under 65, not disabled): tax credit of up to $300 based on property value. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Tier 2 (age 65+ or totally disabled by Jan 1): exempt from taxes on the first $7,500 of assessed value; DOR FAQ states first $75,000 of true value. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; Property Tax FAQ; source)
  • Tier 3 total exemption covers service-connected totally disabled veterans, veterans 90+, and unremarried surviving spouses of those killed on active duty. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Once allowed, exemption carries over each year unless there is a change in ownership, use, occupancy or description (including deed changes, marriage, divorce, death) - reapplication may be required. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Exemption can be disallowed retroactively, e.g. for income tax noncompliance, or claiming homestead on more than one property. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is the Mississippi homestead exemption?

It is a property tax exemption that can lower the yearly tax on your primary home. The Department of Revenue says homeowners must apply and must meet every eligibility requirement, and the amount depends on which of three tiers you qualify for.

The rules are in Mississippi Code Sections 27-33-1 through 27-33-79. Failing any requirement can cost you the exemption retroactively, which matters if you plan to sell and the buyer or lender looks at the tax history.

The exemption affects the tax bill only. It does not change what the house is worth or what a buyer pays for it.

Who qualifies, and when do you apply?

You apply in person at the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and you must own and occupy the home as your primary residence on January 1. Applications are accepted only at the assessor's office during normal business hours, and the state's FAQ says a missed April 1 deadline means you do not qualify for that assessment year.

  • Ownership must be established before January 1, and the ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7.
  • You must meet the definition of head of family in Section 27-33-13 and own the property in a way recognized by Section 27-33-17.
  • You and your spouse must comply with Mississippi income tax law and the road and bridge privilege tax law.
  • Military personnel stationed outside Mississippi can qualify if they claim Mississippi residency and comply with state law. A married servicemember needs both spouses to qualify.

Bring Social Security numbers or ITINs for all applicants, dates of birth, contact information, the property's physical address, the purchase price and down payment, a HUD closing statement or similar documents, and the tag numbers of all vehicles. A P.O. box cannot be used as the property address.

How much does each tier save?

TierWho it coversBenefit
Tier 1, regularQualified applicants under 65 who do not qualify for a disability tierTax credit of up to $300, based on property value
Tier 2, age or disabilityAt least 65 or totally disabled by January 1 of the filing yearExempt from tax on the first $7,500 of assessed value
Tier 3, totalService-connected totally disabled honorably discharged veterans, veterans 90 or older, and certain unremarried surviving spousesExempt from all property taxes on the qualifying homestead

The Department of Revenue FAQ describes the Tier 2 benefit as an exemption on the first $75,000 of true value. A single-family owner-occupied home is assessed at 10 percent, so $75,000 of true value equals $7,500 of assessed value. After the first year, the Tier 2 exemption can grow to include most later increases in value.

Tier 2 applicants need proof of age, such as a driver's license or birth certificate, or proof of total disability. Accepted disability proof includes a Social Security Act classification, a Railroad Retirement Act classification, a qualified retirement plan classification, IRS Schedule 3 and Schedule R, or a detailed letter from two physicians.

What does the exemption look like on an actual tax bill?

Using the state's own sample numbers, a $100,000 home in Class I has an assessed value of $10,000, and at 125 mills the tax due is $1,250. The Department of Revenue publishes that example in its local property appraisal guide, and millage varies by county, city, and school district.

Applying the Tier 2 rule to that same example is our own illustration, not a state figure. The first $7,500 of assessed value is exempt, which leaves $2,500 taxable, and at 125 mills the tax comes to $312.50 instead of $1,250. A Tier 1 homeowner would instead receive a credit of up to $300 against the $1,250.

Property tax is figured as true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. Check your own bill with the county Tax Collector, because the rate in your tax district drives the result.

Do you have to reapply every year?

No, but certain changes force a new application. Once a valid application is on file, the credit repeats each year unless the applicant loses the exemption or something changes since January 1 of the preceding year.

  • A change in property description, ownership, use, or occupancy.
  • Marriage, divorce, remarriage, death, or a deed change.
  • A change in eligibility for disability or Veterans Affairs benefits.
  • Moving into a different tier, such as turning 65, which requires reapplying in the next filing period.

When in doubt, call the county Tax Assessor and ask before April 1. A late application cannot be rescued with a refund for that assessment year.

How can you lose the exemption?

The exemption can be disallowed for any lapse in the underlying rules, and the cost can come back to you. The Department of Revenue lists common reasons:

  • Not filing or not paying Mississippi income tax on time, or filing as a non-resident.
  • Failing to register vehicles properly. The FAQ explains that vehicles must be tagged where they are domiciled, and that is the homestead property.
  • Claiming homestead on more than one property.
  • Not reapplying after a change in description, ownership, use, or occupancy.

A disallowance can require you to repay the tax jurisdictions for the exemption received in error. The department warns this can affect future assessments, mortgage payments, and escrow payments, and can lead to collection efforts. A buyer's lender may ask about it, so clear up any dispute before you list.

What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?

It stays with the owner, not the house. A change in ownership is one of the events that requires a new application, so the buyer must apply during the next January 1 to April 1 window if they will live there.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1, taxes are billed in November and December, and payment is due by February 1. If you sell in the middle of the year, ask the closing agent how that year's taxes will be split. This guide cannot confirm a standard proration rule, so rely on the contract and the title company.

A seller who moved out and rented the house should not expect to keep claiming the exemption, since the applicant must live there on January 1. Class II assessment at 15 percent applies to real property that is not single-family owner-occupied. A cash buyer purchasing as-is will also want to see that taxes are current, since unpaid balances can lead to the county tax sale and a two-year redemption period under Section 27-45-3.

More questions about Mississippi Homestead Exemption

When is the Mississippi homestead exemption deadline?

April 1. Applications are accepted only at the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and you must have owned and lived in the home on January 1.

How much is the homestead exemption in Mississippi?

It depends on the tier. Tier 1 gives a credit of up to $300, Tier 2 exempts the first $7,500 of assessed value for people 65 or older or totally disabled, and Tier 3 exempts all property tax for qualifying veterans and certain surviving spouses.

Do I need to reapply for the homestead exemption every year?

No. Once approved, it carries forward unless ownership, use, occupancy, or the property description changes, or you qualify for a different tier.

Can I keep the exemption if I rent out my house?

The applicant must own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. Check with the county Tax Assessor before you claim it for a rented house, because claiming it incorrectly can lead to disallowance.

Does the buyer get my homestead exemption?

No. A change in ownership requires a new application. The buyer must file with the county Tax Assessor during the next January 1 to April 1 window.

title: Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Mississippi does not have an inheritance tax nor a gift tax. (Estate | MS DOR; source)
  • For decedents dying after 2004, the state death tax credit is replaced with a deduction for state death taxes. (Estate | MS DOR; source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Mississippi have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

No. The Mississippi Department of Revenue states that Mississippi does not have an inheritance tax nor a gift tax, and that no state estate tax return is required for anyone who died on or after January 1, 2005.

Before 2005 the state collected an estate tax built on a federal credit for state death taxes. For deaths after 2004 that credit became a deduction on the federal return, so the state tax effectively went away. The old estate tax laws still sit in Title 27, Chapter 9 of the Mississippi Code, and the Uniform Estate Tax Apportionment Act is in Title 27, Chapter 10.

For an heir who wants to sell a Mississippi house, that means nobody will send you a state bill just because the house passed to you. The costs that do show up are federal rules for very large estates, income tax on any gain after the sale, property tax on the land, and the ordinary expense of recording the paperwork.

Where could the federal estate tax apply to a Mississippi home?

The federal estate tax only reaches estates above a high exclusion amount. The IRS lists a filing threshold of $15,000,000 for a 2026 year of death, and the Form 706 instructions give the same basic exclusion amount along with a basic credit amount of $5,945,800.

The same instructions put the annual gift exclusion at $19,000 per recipient for 2025 through 2026. Those numbers belong to the person who died, not to the heir, and the executor is the one who files if a return is needed.

A typical family house in Mississippi is far below that line. The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing units of $169,800 for 2020 to 2024. A house would only matter for the federal tax if the whole estate, counting every account and asset, passed the threshold.

Mississippi and federal estate tax facts at a glance

ItemWhat the official source saysSource
State estate tax returnNot required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005Mississippi Department of Revenue
State inheritance taxNoneMississippi Department of Revenue
State gift taxNoneMississippi Department of Revenue
Federal filing threshold, 2026 deaths$15,000,000IRS
Federal basic credit amount, 2026$5,945,800IRS Form 706 instructions
Annual gift exclusion, 2025 to 2026$19,000 per doneeIRS Form 706 instructions
Median owner-occupied home value, 2020 to 2024$169,800U.S. Census Bureau

What does an heir owe in income tax when selling an inherited house?

An heir owes income tax only on the gain, and the starting point is the basis. The IRS explains that the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally its fair market value on the date of death, whether or not the executor files an estate tax return.

If the sale price is above that basis, the difference is a taxable gain. If you report a sale, it goes on Schedule D and Form 8949 of the federal return. The IRS also notes that an executor who files Form 706 may give heirs a Schedule A to Form 8971, and in that case your basis may have to match the value finally used for estate tax purposes.

This is why a date-of-death value matters even when no estate tax is due. Heirs who plan to sell often get a written appraisal for that date, because it fixes the number the gain is measured against. Ask the executor or a tax professional which value applies to your situation.

  • Keep the date-of-death appraisal or valuation letter with the sale file.
  • Keep closing statements, since selling costs reduce the gain.
  • Ask the executor whether a Schedule A to Form 8971 was issued.

How do property taxes work on an inherited Mississippi house?

Property tax follows the house, not the estate. The Department of Revenue says property is assessed each year to the owner of record on January 1, the bill is issued in November or December, and the tax is due by the following February 1.

If a parent dies in the fall and the house sits in the estate, the tax for that year still has to be paid by the date it comes due. Taxes paid to the county Tax Collector are calculated as true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. A single-family, owner-occupied house is Class I at 10 percent of true value. An inherited house that nobody lives in is no longer owner-occupied, so it would fall into the 15 percent class for all other real property.

Unpaid taxes carry real consequences. The state FAQ says property with delinquent taxes can be sold at the county tax auction, and Mississippi gives the owner two years after the sale to redeem the property under Section 27-45-3. A house that has sat unpaid for several years is worth checking before you list it.

What happens to the homestead exemption when the owner dies?

The exemption does not pass to the heirs on its own. The Department of Revenue says a homestead exemption stays in place from year to year unless something changes, and death, deed changes, and changes in occupancy are listed as events that can require a new application.

For a buyer or heir, the filing window is January 1 through April 1 at the county Tax Assessor, and the applicant must own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. Our Mississippi homestead exemption guide covers the tiers. If you sell, the new owner has to apply on their own.

Who handles the estate and the deed before a sale?

In Mississippi the county chancery clerk handles both the estate file and the land records. A county chancery clerk office describes its Chancery Court role as covering estates, guardianships, conservatorships, divorces and other equity matters, and its Recording Department records deeds, deeds of trust, releases, liens, and lis pendens.

The Department of Revenue describes the chancery clerk as the custodian of public land records, and those records are what the assessor uses to learn who owns a parcel. A new deed to the heirs or to a buyer needs to be recorded so the tax rolls match the real owner.

Recording fees are set by statute. One county clerk's schedule, effective January 1, 2020 under Section 25-7-9, lists deeds at $26.00 in an archive-fee county or $25.00 in a non-archive county for the first five pages, plus $1.00 for each extra page. Confirm the current amount with the county clerk where the house sits.

What should heirs check before selling a Mississippi house?

Start with the title, then the tax bill, then the buyer. Mississippi has no state estate tax to clear first, so the practical hurdles are paperwork and any liens.

  • Confirm who has legal authority to sign. This usually runs through the chancery court estate file.
  • Pull the county tax record and ask the Tax Collector whether anything is delinquent.
  • Check whether the house was in a tax sale and whether the two-year redemption window is still open.
  • Get a date-of-death value for the basis.
  • Ask the clerk what a deed will cost to record.
  • Ask the closing agent how this year's property tax will be divided between seller and buyer.

A cash buyer can purchase an inherited house as-is, which matters when the home needs repairs the family does not want to fund. That does not remove any of the steps above, and a buyer should not promise a price before the title and liens are known.

More questions about Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there an inheritance tax in Mississippi?

No. The Mississippi Department of Revenue says the state has no inheritance tax and no gift tax, and no state estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

When does the federal estate tax apply to a Mississippi estate?

Only when the estate is large. The IRS lists a $15,000,000 filing threshold for a 2026 year of death. Most single-family homes in the state are valued far below that, though the threshold counts the entire estate.

Do I pay tax when I sell a house I inherited in Mississippi?

You may owe federal income tax on any gain. The IRS says inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death, so the gain is the sale price above that figure.

Who pays the property tax on a house in an estate?

Whoever holds the house when the bill is due. Mississippi assesses the owner of record on January 1, and taxes are due by February 1 of the next year. The estate or the heirs should confirm the balance with the county Tax Collector.

Does the homestead exemption transfer to my heirs?

Not automatically. The Department of Revenue lists death and deed changes among the events that can require a new application, and the filing window is January 1 to April 1 each year.

What the official sources say

  • Residential material noncompliance: landlord may give written notice terminating the rental agreement not less than 14 days after receipt if not remedied within 14 days; notice may be by email/text if agreed in writing. (Miss. Code 89-8-13(3) as in SB 2461 (2022); source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by written notice at least 30 days before termination; week-to-week by 7 days. (Miss. Code 89-8-19 as in SB 2461 (2022); source)
  • For nonpayment of rent, written notice requiring payment or possession after 3 days (89-7-27). (MS AG Consumer Guide (quotes 89-7-27); source)
  • Landlord files a sworn affidavit with the court; summons issues with a hearing not less than 3 nor more than 5 days from the summons date (89-7-31). (MS AG Consumer Guide (quotes 89-7-31); source)
  • Eviction hearing adjournments cannot extend the hearing beyond 45 days from filing. (MS AG Consumer Guide; source)
  • If judgment is for landlord the court issues a warrant to the sheriff/constable to put the landlord in possession; nonpayment warrant stayed if full rent, late fees and costs are paid within 10 days. (MS AG Consumer Guide (89-7-41, 89-7-45); source)
  • Tenant may appeal to circuit court within 30 days after possession is delivered by notice and bond. (MS AG Consumer Guide; source)
  • Residential landlord-tenant rights, notice and eviction rules (89-8, 89-7) apply to occupants; holdover tenants can be removed through the justice-court process described under eviction-process. (MS AG Consumer Guide: Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy needs 30 days' written notice to terminate. (Miss. Code 89-8-19 as in SB 2461 (2022); source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does a residential eviction work in Mississippi?

A landlord must give written notice, file a sworn affidavit or complaint in court, win a judgment, and then have the sheriff or a constable carry out a warrant of removal. The rules for homes and apartments sit in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 89, Chapter 8 of the Mississippi Code.

That chapter was rewritten in 2022 and amended again in 2025, so older summaries can be out of date. Section 89-8-31 says a landlord may start eviction proceedings for breach of the rental agreement or for failing to vacate after the agreement ends. Nothing in the chapter lets an owner skip the court step.

The older Chapter 7 sections, including 89-7-27, apply to premises that are not a dwelling unit, such as commercial space. If you own a rented house, Chapter 8 is the one that governs.

What notice does a Mississippi landlord have to give?

The notice period depends on why the tenancy is ending. Notice must be in writing, and email or text counts only if the tenant agreed in writing to be notified that way.

SituationNotice requiredStatute
Unpaid rentWritten notice that the agreement ends if rent is not paid within 3 days89-8-13(5)
Other material breach by tenantTermination date not less than 14 days after receipt, if not fixed within a reasonable time up to 14 days89-8-13(3)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days written notice89-8-19(3)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days written notice89-8-19(2)
Substantial violation affecting health or safetyNo notice required89-8-19(4)

A breach that can be repaired is treated differently. Under Section 89-8-13, if the tenant fixes the problem before the date in the notice, the rental agreement does not end. If substantially the same breach comes back within six months, the landlord may terminate on at least 14 days of notice.

Unless a lease sets a fixed term, tenancy is week to week for tenants who pay weekly and month to month in every other case. A landlord who sells to a buyer wanting the house vacant often ends up using the month-to-month notice.

What does a landlord file to start the case?

The landlord files a sworn affidavit or complaint and a copy of the notice that was delivered. Section 89-8-33 says the affidavit must state the facts requiring removal and identify the dwelling address and any rent or fees owed.

After filing, the court issues a summons. Section 89-8-35 requires the summons to tell the tenant that the judge will decide whether the landlord is entitled to possession, that a tenant who loses has at least seven days from the judgment to move out unless the judge sets a different period, and that a tenant sued for nonpayment can stop the eviction by paying everything owed. Service follows the Mississippi Rules of Court.

How long does the hearing take and what can the judge order?

The statute puts a hard outer limit on the hearing. Section 89-8-41 allows either side to ask for an adjournment, but a single adjournment cannot exceed ten days unless both parties consent, and no adjournment can push the entire hearing past 30 days from the date the case was filed.

Other points the statute sets out:

  • The court must grant a default judgment if the landlord filed the required papers, the summons was properly served, and the tenant did not appear (89-8-37).
  • Judgments must be signed and executed on the same business day they are granted.
  • If the landlord wins, the judge orders the tenant to vacate within seven days unless an emergency or other compelling circumstance justifies a shorter or longer period (89-8-39).
  • A shorter period can be justified when the tenant committed a substantial health or safety violation or poses an immediate risk of damage or injury.

Check the current text of the statute and confirm timing with the court clerk in the county where the house is, since the chapter was amended in 2022 and again in 2025.

What happens after the move-out date passes?

Only law enforcement can remove a tenant, and only under a warrant. After the court-ordered move-out date the landlord may request a warrant of removal, and on payment of fees the judge issues it to the sheriff or a constable of the county.

The statute adds details that matter to owners. A warrant is not executed when it is simply posted on the door. Officers must remove the occupants and put the landlord in physical possession. For 72 hours afterward the landlord must give the tenant reasonable access to collect belongings. After that, remaining property may be moved to the curb or another agreed location.

In a case based only on unpaid rent, Section 89-8-39 bars the warrant if the tenant has paid in full all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the move-out date, and it obliges the landlord to accept that payment in good faith. Appeals follow the Mississippi Rules of Court under 89-8-43.

How does an eviction affect selling a rented house in Mississippi?

It affects timing, cost, and what condition the house is in when you hand it over. A landlord who wants to sell has three realistic paths, and each one has a different clock.

  • Give a notice to end the tenancy, then sell once the house is vacant.
  • File for eviction because of unpaid rent or a breach, then sell after possession is returned.
  • Sell the house with the tenant in place and let the buyer deal with the lease.

Read the lease before choosing the third path. This guide cannot confirm a statewide rule for how an existing lease binds a new owner, so have an attorney or the title company review it. Do not shut off utilities, change locks, or remove belongings to force a move. The statute routes possession through a court judgment and a warrant.

A cash buyer can buy a rented house as-is, including one that needs repairs after a difficult tenancy. The sale does not remove any court deadline that has already started, and nobody should promise you a closing date until the possession question is clear.

How do property tax classes change when a house is a rental?

A rented single-family house is taxed differently from the owner's own home. The Department of Revenue defines Class I as single-family, owner-occupied residential real property assessed at 10 percent of true value, and Class II as all other real property at 15 percent.

Homestead exemption also requires that the applicant own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. A landlord who moves out and rents the house generally cannot keep claiming it. The assessor makes the final call, so ask the county Tax Assessor if you are unsure.

Property tax is due by February 1 for the preceding assessment year, and an unpaid balance can lead to the county tax sale. Check for a delinquent balance before you list a rental, especially if the tenant stopped paying and the house sat in dispute for months.

More questions about Mississippi Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How many days notice is needed to evict for unpaid rent in Mississippi?

Three days. Under Section 89-8-13(5) the landlord delivers written notice that the rental agreement will end if rent is not paid within three days. Email or text works only if the tenant agreed in writing.

How long does a Mississippi eviction take?

The hearing cannot be adjourned beyond 30 days from the filing date under Section 89-8-41, and a tenant who loses generally gets seven days to move out. Total time also depends on notice, service, and how soon the sheriff or constable acts on the warrant.

Can a landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. The statute provides a court judgment and a warrant of removal served by the sheriff or a constable. A warrant posted on the door is not executed, and officers must physically put the landlord in possession.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?

In a nonpayment case, yes. Section 89-8-39 says the judge shall not issue a warrant if the tenant paid all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the court-ordered move-out date, and the landlord must accept that payment in good faith.

Do different rules apply to commercial tenants?

Yes. Section 89-7-27 covers premises that are not a dwelling unit and allows removal after default in rent and three days of written notice, among other grounds. Residential cases use Chapter 8.

Mississippi Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Mississippi Quitclaim Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Any interest in or claim to land may be conveyed by a writing signed and delivered, and an instrument is construed to carry out the parties' manifest intent even if technically imperfect. (Mississippi Supreme Court opinion (CO124366) quoting 89-1-1; source)
  • Chancery Clerk is custodian of public land records and receives, records and maintains all land ownership records. (Local Property Appraisal - Chancery Clerks; source)
  • Any interest in land may be conveyed by a writing signed and delivered (Miss. Code 89-1-1). (Mississippi Supreme Court opinion (CO124366); source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where is a quitclaim deed recorded in Mississippi?

A quitclaim deed is recorded with the chancery clerk of the county where the land is located. Miss. Code 89-5-1 says a conveyance of land is not good against a purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, or against any creditor, unless it is lodged with the clerk of the chancery court of the county where the lands are situated.

The Department of Revenue describes the chancery clerk as the custodian of public land records, the office that receives, records and maintains all land ownership records. Tax assessors use those records to learn who owns a property, and tax collectors use them to learn who owes the tax. So a deed that never reaches the clerk can leave the tax bill in the old owner's name.

County offices differ on how they take documents. The Rankin County Chancery Clerk's site, for example, lists separate topics for recording requirements and e-recording, so check the clerk's page for the county before you drive to the courthouse.

What happens if a Mississippi quitclaim deed is not recorded?

An unrecorded deed still binds the people who signed it, but it can lose to someone who records first. Under 89-5-3, conveyances of land are void as to creditors and subsequent purchasers for valuable consideration without notice unless they are acknowledged or proved and lodged with the chancery clerk.

The same section says that as between the parties and their heirs, and as to later purchasers with notice or without valuable consideration, the instrument stays valid and binding. It also says priority is decided by the order of filing, in the absence of actual notice.

  • Recording protects the person who received the deed.
  • Priority runs by time of filing, so a delay can matter if two deeds exist for one house.
  • A deed has to be acknowledged or proved before it is lodged for record.

This is the reason title companies ask for recorded deeds in the chain of title. If a house was handed from parent to child by an unrecorded quitclaim years ago, a buyer will want that fixed first.

What format rules apply to a deed presented for recording?

Mississippi sets physical format standards in Miss. Code 89-5-24, and a deed that does not meet them can still be recorded for an extra fee. The statute adds $10 per document or instrument for a deed that does not substantially conform, and says a format failure does not affect validity or enforceability.

RequirementWhat 89-5-24 says
PagesPrinted on one side only, not permanently bound
Type sizeNo smaller than ten-point
PaperWhite, not less than twenty-pound weight
SignaturesBlack or blue ink, with the name typed or printed beneath
First page top marginAt least three inches reserved for the recorder
Other marginsAt least three-fourths of an inch

The first page, below the three-inch margin, must carry the name, business mailing address and business or employment telephone number of the person who prepared the document, plus the name, mailing address and phone number of every grantor and grantee. It also needs a return address, the document title and the legal description or indexing instruction.

Exempt categories include documents executed before July 1, 2009, certified copies from a court or agency, and documents where one of the original parties is deceased or incapacitated. The Harrison County Chancery Clerk's website adds that, because of the amended section, that office will not accept handwritten documents.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Mississippi?

Recording a quitclaim deed costs $25 in counties that do not collect the archive fee and $26 in those that do, for up to five pages. The fee schedule, published by the Mississippi Chancery Clerk's Association and posted on the Harrison County Chancery Clerk's site, reflects changes effective January 1, 2020 under Miss. Code 25-7-9.

ItemArchive-fee countyNon-archive county
Quitclaim deed, first five pages, with indexing$26.00$25.00
Each page beyond five$1.00$1.00
Nonconforming format surcharge (89-5-24)$10.00$10.00

The schedule lists Rankin, Hinds, Madison, Lowndes and Harrison among the counties collecting the $1 archive fee. DeSoto is not on that list. The schedule also notes mineral stamp fees where they apply, with a $1.00 minimum, and the clerk says actual fees are calculated at recording and may differ from an online estimate. Call the clerk before you send a check.

How does a quitclaim deed affect homestead exemption and the tax bill?

A change of ownership can require a new homestead application. The Department of Revenue lists deed changes among the events, with marriage, divorce and death, that can trigger the need to reapply.

The same page says owners must own and occupy the home on January 1 of the year they claim the exemption. The ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7 for that year. Applications go to the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1.

  • Because of the January 7 filing rule, the timing of a family deed can matter for that year's exemption.
  • Disallowance can mean repaying the exemption received in error.
  • Property tax is assessed to the owner of record on January 1 and due by February 1.

Our Mississippi homestead exemption guide and property tax guide go further into these dates.

When does a quitclaim deed help in a house sale, and when does it fall short?

A quitclaim deed is a tool for moving an interest between people, and it does not by itself answer whether the signer has authority to sell. Whether it works for a sale depends on who is on title and what court steps are still open.

  • Between family members who already own the house, it can add or remove a name from title, if the deed is properly acknowledged and recorded.
  • For an inherited house, the heirs usually have to deal with the estate first. See our Mississippi probate guide.
  • When a spouse or co-owner is involved, ask a Mississippi attorney about marital and homestead rights before anyone signs.
  • If a loan or tax lien is attached to the house, ask the title company how it will be paid off before closing.

The sources we reviewed explain recording and format. They do not address warranties or title insurance on a quitclaim, so ask a Mississippi real estate attorney or title company before you rely on one in a sale.

We buy Mississippi houses as-is and reply with a written offer. If the deed is the open question, we can talk through what the chancery clerk's records show before anyone signs.

More questions about Mississippi Quitclaim Deed

Is a quitclaim deed valid in Mississippi if it is not recorded?

It is valid between the people who signed it and their heirs. Under section 89-5-3 it can lose to a later purchaser for value without notice, or to a creditor, if it was not lodged with the chancery clerk.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Mississippi?

For a quitclaim deed the published fee is $25 in non-archive counties and $26 in archive-fee counties for the first five pages, plus $1 for each extra page. The clerk calculates the final amount at recording.

What must be on the first page of a Mississippi deed?

The preparer's name, business address and phone, and the name, address and phone of each grantor and grantee, plus a return address, the title and the legal description, all below a three-inch top margin.

Do I need a notary for a quitclaim deed in Mississippi?

Section 89-5-3 requires a conveyance to be acknowledged or proved before it is lodged with the clerk, if it is to be good against creditors and later purchasers. Ask the clerk's office who can take the acknowledgment.

Will a quitclaim deed change my homestead exemption?

It can. The Department of Revenue says deed changes may require a new homestead application, and the ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7 of the year the exemption is claimed.

title: Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property
content:
Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A will devising Mississippi real property may be admitted to probate as a muniment of title only, by petition signed by all beneficiaries and the spouse, without appointing an executor, if the personal probate estate (excluding real property and exempt property) did not exceed $10,000 and known debts are paid. (Miss. Code 91-5-35 (as amended by SB 2850, 2020); source)
  • Successor affidavit: 30 days after death, a successor may collect debts or tangible personal property of the decedent by affidavit if the entire probate estate does not exceed the limit (SB 2850 raised it from $50,000 to $75,000). (Miss. Code 91-7-322 (as amended by SB 2850, 2020); source)
  • The affidavit must state no personal representative petition is pending or appointed, and the affiant's relationship to the decedent. (Miss. Code 91-7-322 (via SB 2850); source)
Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which court handles probate in Mississippi?

Probate in Mississippi runs through the chancery court of a county, and the county depends on where the decedent lived. Under Miss. Code 91-7-1, a will is proved and letters testamentary are granted by the chancery court of the county where the testator had a fixed place of residence.

If the testator had no fixed residence and the will devises land, the proper court is the chancery court of the county where the land, or some part of it, sits. For someone who died without a will, Miss. Code 91-7-63 points to the chancery court of the county where the person lived at death. If there was no fixed residence, it points to the county where the person died or where some of the personal property is.

The statute that sets the scope of the chapter, 91-1-1, says it applies to property of decedents domiciled in Mississippi and to real property of nonresidents located in the state. So an heir living in another state who inherits a Mississippi house still deals with a Mississippi chancery court for that house.

What are the probate routes for a Mississippi estate that owns a house?

There are three routes that matter to a house owner's heirs: full administration, a will admitted as a muniment of title only, and a successor affidavit for small personal property. Only the first two can touch real estate.

RouteWhat it doesLimit or triggerSource
Letters testamentaryCourt admits the will and appoints an executorChancery court of the county of residence91-7-1
Letters of administrationCourt appoints an administrator when there is no willRelative preferred, then others; creditor or other suitable person after 30 days91-7-63
Muniment of title onlyWill admitted to clear title to devised real property without an executor or administratorProbate estate within the 91-7-322 limit, known debts paid91-5-35
Successor affidavitSuccessor collects debts or tangible personal propertyEntire probate estate no more than $75,000, at least 30 days after death91-7-322

The affidavit route reaches debts owed to the decedent and tangible personal property, such as a bank balance or a vehicle. The text of 91-7-322 does not mention conveying real property, so a house generally needs one of the court routes.

How does a will admitted as a muniment of title work?

A muniment of title petition lets a will that devises Mississippi land be admitted without appointing an executor or administrator. The 2020 amendment in Senate Bill 2850 rewrote section 91-5-35 and took effect July 1, 2020.

The petition must be signed and sworn by the personal representative. If no executor, administrator with the will annexed, or foreign personal representative is serving, it is signed and sworn by the decedent's living spouse and by the devisees of the Mississippi real property, whether specific or residuary. People holding only contingent remainder interests are left out.

The petition must show two things:

  • The decedent's probate estate in Mississippi, not counting real property and exempt property, stayed within the amount set in section 91-7-322, which SB 2850 raised from $50,000 to $75,000.
  • All known debts of the decedent and the estate are paid, including estate and income taxes if any.

Older summaries, including some quoted online, still say $10,000. That figure was in the pre-2020 text and was replaced. A muniment of title also does not shut the door on others: an interested party can still petition for formal administration or contest the will.

Who gets appointed when there is no will?

When someone dies intestate, the chancery court grants letters of administration to a relative who applies, and the husband or wife comes first. Under 91-7-63, the court then looks to others next entitled to share in the estate, choosing among equals the person best suited to manage it.

The statute also lets the court select a stranger, or a trust company or national bank doing business in Mississippi, if the kindred are incompetent. If no relative applies within 30 days of death, the court may grant administration to a creditor or another suitable person. For a family hoping to sell a house, that 30-day mark matters, because a creditor can end up in control of the process if relatives wait.

How do creditor claims affect the sale of an inherited house?

Creditor claims have a short clock in Mississippi, and an unresolved claim can hold up the estate even when the house itself has equity. Under 91-7-145, the executor or administrator must make reasonably diligent efforts to identify creditors and mail each one a notice.

The representative then files an affidavit with the clerk and publishes a notice in a county newspaper for three consecutive weeks. The notice tells creditors that a claim not probated and registered within 90 days after first publication will be barred. Section 91-7-151, as quoted in the 2018 bill text and in Mississippi Supreme Court opinions, says the same ninety-day rule bars late claims.

If no newspaper is published in the county, posting at the courthouse door and three other places of public resort is enough. Proof of publication has to be filed before a decree of final discharge.

For heirs, the practical result is a timeline you can plan around:

  • Letters issued by the chancery court start the notice process.
  • Three weeks of publication, then 90 days from first publication for claims.
  • Known debts, taxes and any mortgage on the house still have to be dealt with before heirs see net proceeds.

What do heirs usually face when selling an inherited house in Mississippi?

The common problems are unclear title, carrying costs while the court works, and a house that needs repairs nobody wants to pay for. Property tax is a good example of a cost that keeps running. The Mississippi Department of Revenue explains that taxes are assessed to the owner of record on January 1, billed in November or December, and due by the following February 1.

A death in the middle of the year does not pause that cycle. Our Mississippi property tax guide covers the bill, appeals and tax sale timing.

Recording matters too. Under 89-5-3, a conveyance is void against creditors and later purchasers for value without notice unless it is acknowledged or proved and lodged with the chancery clerk of the proper county. As between the parties and their heirs, the instrument stays valid either way. Heirs who sign deeds among themselves should still record them.

  • Confirm which chancery court has the estate and who holds letters.
  • Ask the chancery clerk where the will and any petitions are filed.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, the deed into the decedent and a recent tax bill.
  • Check whether the house has a mortgage, tax arrears or liens.

How does a cash sale fit with Mississippi probate?

A cash buyer does not replace probate. It changes how the house is sold once the person with authority to sign is clear. A personal representative with letters, or heirs who hold title after a muniment of title, can sign a deed, and the buyer can take the house as it stands.

That can help when the house is vacant, has deferred repairs or sits in a county far from the heirs. We buy houses in Mississippi as-is and respond with a written offer. We do not promise a price here, and we recommend talking to a Mississippi probate attorney about which route fits your estate.

More questions about Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I have to probate a will in Mississippi if the house is in the will?

Usually yes. A will that devises Mississippi real property is proved in chancery court, either with letters testamentary or, for smaller estates, as a muniment of title under section 91-5-35. The right route depends on the size of the probate estate and whether debts are paid.

What is the small estate limit for a successor affidavit in Mississippi?

The limit is $75,000 for the entire probate estate. Section 91-7-322 was amended by SB 2850, effective July 1, 2020, and the affidavit can be used at least 30 days after death. It covers debts owed to the decedent and tangible personal property, not real estate.

How long do creditors have to file claims against a Mississippi estate?

Creditors have 90 days after the first publication of the notice to present a claim. The notice must run for three consecutive weeks, and known creditors must also be mailed notice.

Which county's chancery court handles my parent's estate?

Generally the county where your parent had a fixed place of residence at death. If there was no fixed residence and the will devises land, it is the county where the land lies.

Can a nonresident heir sell inherited Mississippi property?

Yes, but the real property of a decedent is still handled under Mississippi law and a Mississippi court. An out-of-state heir should work with the chancery clerk's office or a Mississippi attorney to confirm who signs the deed.
